abstract: We describe our work for the CALCS 2018 shared task on named entity recognition on code-switched data. Our system ranked first place for MS Arabic-Egyptian named entity recognition and third place for English-Spanish.

bibliographic.title: Code-Switched Named Entity Recognition with Embedding Attention
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the Third Workshop on Computational Approaches to Code-Switching

content.problem: Multilingual speakers frequently alternate between languages (code-switching), and traditional monolingual NLP techniques, including named entity recognition systems, degrade sharply on such mixed-language social media input.
content.proposed_solution: The authors build a neural NER system that combines pre-trained FastText word embeddings, character-level BiLSTM representations, a learned self-attention over these multiple embeddings, explicit capitalization features, and a shortcut-stacked BiLSTM encoder feeding a CRF tagger.
content.algorithm_or_model: shortcut-stacked BiLSTM-CRF with embedding-level self-attention over multilingual FastText and character-level embeddings
dataset_testbed: CALCS 2018 shared task Modern Standard Arabic-Egyptian (MSA-EGY) Twitter NER dataset
CALCS 2018 shared task English-Spanish (ENG-SPA) Twitter NER dataset

content.claim: Their attention-based neural system beat a simpler embedding-concatenation baseline on the test sets of both language pairs, earning first place in the shared task for MSA-Egyptian and third place for English-Spanish.
author_stated_limitations: The very small ENG-SPA development set (832 tweets versus a 15.6k test set) made dev and test performance diverge and made hyperparameter tuning difficult.
They only tried a simple ensembling strategy and did not pursue proper ensembling because of time constraints.
They felt a strong gazetteer could have helped, although they believed relying on it would defeat the purpose of their general neural architecture.
The very poor performance on the OTHER category for ENG-SPA might be an artifact of that category being small.

evidence.problem_quote: The tendency for multilingual speakers to engage in code-switching—i.e, alternating between multiple languages or language varieties—poses important problems for NLP systems: traditional monolingual techniques quickly break down with input from mixed languages.
evidence.proposed_solution_quote: In this paper, we exploit recent advances in neural NLP systems, tailored to code-switching. We use high-quality FastText embeddings trained on Common Crawl (Grave et al., 2018; Mikolov et al., 2018) and employ shortcut-stacked sentence encoders (Nie and Bansal, 2017) to obtain deep token-level representations to feed into the CRF.
evidence.claim_quote: Our system ranked first place for MS Arabic-Egyptian named entity recognition and third place for English-Spanish.
author_stated_limitation_quotes: The dev set for this task was very small (832, versus a test set of 15.6k), which explains the discrepancy between dev set and test set performance—this discrepancy also made it difficult to tune hyperparameters properly for this task.
We did not pursue proper ensembling due to time constraints.

We felt that we could have benefited from having a strong gazetteer, but also believe that this would kind of defeat the purpose of our general neural network architecture, which should not have to rely on those kinds of features.
The Other category was perfectly handled for MSA-EGY, while this was very bad for ENG-SPA — this could however also be an artifact, since that category was quite small.
